title: Mathematical Platonism
content_html:
Mathematical Platonism

Mathematical Platonism or, more recently, the Mathematical Universe Hypothesis (MUH) originates with Plato: mathematical objects (numbers, forms, geometrical structures) exist independently of the physical world. In this view, reality is fundamentally mathematical form; what we see is a shadow or imperfect instance of these ideal forms. Many mathematicians (e.g. Gödel) leaned toward this, claiming mathematics “discovers” rather than “invents” truth.

The Pythagoreans already claimed “all is number.” - the world is fundamentally ratios, symmetries, and structures that can be expressed mathematically. Max Tegmark’s Mathematical Universe Hypothesis (MUH) takes this idea and proposes that the external physical world is a mathematical structure, not just described by mathematics, but identical to it. Every consistent mathematical structure exists as a universe. What science ultimately reveals is not “things” but the mathematical relations between them. Matter may be secondary; structure is primary.

However, mathematics is an abstract language; it predicts, but why should the universe be it? If reality is just math, why do we experience qualia, embodiment, temporality? If every mathematical structure exists, how do we explain why we inhabit this one?

Modern philosophy of mathematics (esp. structuralism) argues that mathematics is not about things but about relations between things. Example: the number “2” has no essence apart from its place in the structure of natural numbers (between 1 and 3, divisible into 1+1, etc.). Similarly, geometry describes relational properties (distances, symmetries), not intrinsic “substances.” In physics, structural realism holds that what science uncovers are not particles as “things-in-themselves,” but the network of relations (laws, symmetries, interactions). Numbers and structures have no meaning outside their relational web, a mathematical entity = its relations to others.

In Buddhism, phenomena have no independent essence; they are constituted by relations, a thing = its conditions, dependencies, and connections. Both these views deny intrinsic, standalone existence, both see reality as relational fabric. To say “reality is mathematics” and “reality is empty/relational” might be different languages for the same insight: there are no self-standing “things,” only patterns of relations. This helps explain why mathematics is so effective at describing nature (Wigner’s “unreasonable effectiveness” problem) - because both mathematics and phenomena are relational at core.

Just as mathematics defines entities by relations, and Buddhism says phenomena lack intrinsic essence, neuroscience shows memory is not a fixed thing stored in the brain. Each memory is constituted by relations between neurons (synaptic patterns), relations between memories (associations, context) and relations between present and past (recall = reconstruction). A memory has no independent essence; it exists only in networks and reconstructions. Each act of memory recall is a branching - a “parallel version” of the past. Reconsolidation means memory isn’t static: it forks and mutates, much like a multiverse of outcomes. Our personal identity is therefore not a single history, but an ensemble of possible remembered pasts.
